newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Protestant truce still operates - Mayhew.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Protestant truce still operates - Mayhew.

text.p: Britain signalled on Monday it considered a shaky truce by Northern Ireland's Protestant "Loyalist" guerrillas was intact despite fears it had been ditched in response to violence by the Irish Republican Army.

"I am very glad that the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), so-called, has not moved back from the ceasefire which it announced 27 months ago," Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew told BBC radio.
"That distinguishes it from the IRA command which ended its ceasefire, evily and quite unjustifiably, in February this year."
Mayhew was speaking in Londonderry city hours after the province's police chief blamed pro-British militants for two recent attacks on Catholics that fanned a new cycle of sectarian violence.
Mayhew said he would adopt a wait-and-see approach to the continued participation of Protestant Loyalist parties, the guerrillas' political wings, in multi-party peace talks that resumed on Monday.

The talks have been overshadowed by burgeoning guerrilla violence and bitter wrangling between rival Protestant and Catholic parties about how to get IRA guerrillas to scrap their weapons if they call a truce.
Britain says the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing will be allowed in only when the guerrillas declare a credible ceasefire.

"I very much hope that the Loyalists will not descend to the evil of a resumed terrorist campaign. It would be profoundly evil, it would be wrong, it would be deeply damaging to the people of this province," Mayhew told BBC radio.
Earlier Royal Ulster Constabulary police chief Ronnie Flanagan blamed pro-British Loyalists for bomb attacks on two Catholics in December.
Flanagan did not name the suspect groups or say whether they were ones that were party to the CLMC truce.

Mainstream pro-British Protestant parties said they would be pressing Britain to brief them on who was behind the suspected Loyalist attacks and on whether Loyalist parties would be allowed to remain at the talks table.
Loyalist parties have seats in the fractious talks because their military allies called a truce in October 1994 in response to a truce which the IRA later abandoned.
Loyalists killed members of the province's Catholic nationalist minority in a bid to thwart an IRA campaign aimed at ending Britain's rule over the province.

"I would think that is the work of Loyalist extremist groups," Flanagan told BBC radio referring to booby-trapped car attacks in December against two leading republicans who oppose British rule over the province.
It was the first security force assessment of what politicians across the sectarian divide had suspected.
One of the bombs exploded and injured a well-known Belfast republican. The other was defused after it was spotted under the car of the other intended victim.
No group has claimed responsibiltiy for the attacks, which appeared to breach a Loyalist truce in force since October 1994.
Loyalist politicians say that the truce is still in place because the guerrillas' CLMC umbrella group has not made any statement that it is over.
